vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: dashpass
Version: 0.5.0

The 'dashpass' skill is a well-documented credential management tool for the Dash Platform. It implements local client-side encryption (AES-256-GCM) using a user-provided master key (WIF) and includes several security best practices, such as zeroing sensitive buffers, using an encrypted local cache with restrictive file permissions (0600), and providing clear documentation on its security model and trust minimization. No evidence of malicious intent, unauthorized data exfiltration, or prompt injection was found in the code (dashpass-cli.mjs) or instructions (SKILL.md).

llm.summary: The skill's requested access (your WIF private key and identity) is proportionate for a blockchain-backed vault, but there are several inconsistencies and subtle risks you should understand before installing.

dimensions.detail: The name/description (encrypted credential vault on Dash) aligns with the code and required env vars: CRITICAL_WIF and DASHPASS_IDENTITY_ID are exactly what a client-side encryption approach needs. Requiring node and the Dash Evo SDK is expected. However, the README language implies the AI 'never sees your key' while the design explicitly returns decrypted plaintext to callers — so the distinction between ‘AI never sees your key’ and ‘AI can receive plaintext via the local system’ is blurred and worth noting.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: SKILL.md and the CLI instruct the agent to perform store/retrieve operations that will decrypt secrets locally and hand plaintext back to the caller. The docs claim 'CRITICAL-level human confirmation' is required before AI access, but the included CLI source shows no enforced interactive gating for critical-level operations (no mandatory human prompt or external approval flow). The skill also writes a local encrypted cache (~/.dashpass/cache) and reads environment variables; these are within scope but increase local attack surface. Metadata (service names, types) is stored on-chain (document acknowledges this).
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no packaged install spec (instruction-only), which minimizes supply-chain risk from installers but requires you to run npm install @dashevo/evo-sdk@3.1.0-dev.1. Installing a development-version SDK is riskier than a pinned stable release — review the exact package version before installing. No remote arbitrary binary downloads are present in the package itself.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: Requesting CRITICAL_WIF (your private key) and DASHPASS_IDENTITY_ID is functionally necessary for the described client-side encryption, so the variables are proportionate in purpose but extremely sensitive. The code reads CRITICAL_WIF and uses it to derive encryption keys and to sign transactions; any compromise of that env var (or the process that exposes it) compromises all vault contents. The skill's documentation repeatedly warns not to paste the WIF in chat, but the agent's ability to call the CLI and receive plaintext means the agent can still obtain stored secrets — which may be surprising given some of the language in the docs.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request always:true and does not modify other skills or system-wide settings. It creates a per-user cache under ~/.dashpass and uses typical file permissions (mode 0600/0700). Autonomy (model invocation) remains enabled by default which is normal; combine this with the sensitive env var and the agent's ability to fetch plaintext and you'll have a larger blast radius — but autonomy alone is not unusual.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: Before installing, consider these points: 1) This skill requires your wallet private key (CRITICAL_WIF) in your environment — if that key is exposed, all vault secrets are compromised. Only use a testnet or dedicated key; never put a mainnet wallet WIF into an agent-accessible environment. 2) The CLI decrypts values locally and will return plaintext to the caller — an agent that can invoke the CLI can obtain secrets. If you expect the AI to be unable to read secrets at all, this is not the case. 3) The docs claim human confirmation is required for CRITICAL items, but the included CLI source does not enforce an interactive approval flow; if you need strict human-in-the-loop approvals, add/verify implementation. 4) The SDK version requested is a dev release (@3.1.0-dev.1); review that package and prefer a stable, audited release where possible. 5) The default contract is a shared testnet contract (metadata like service names will be visible on-chain); set DASHPASS_CONTRACT_ID to your own contract for privacy. 6) Audit the included script (scripts/dashpass-cli.mjs) yourself or have someone you trust do it; verify the code path that handles 'critical' flags, caching behavior, and that it doesn't log secrets. If you proceed, use a throwaway/test identity and testnet WIF first, and back up your WIF securely before trusting this with any real secrets.
